nameStory: Land cress gets its name because it grows on dry land rather than in water like its famous cousin, watercress. It's also called 'poor man's cabbage' because it provided free, nutritious greens to those who couldn't afford store-bought vegetables. The name 'cress' comes from an old Germanic word meaning 'to creep or crawl,' referring to how these plants spread along the ground.
description: Land cress is a low-growing biennial herb that forms rosettes of dark green, deeply lobed leaves close to the ground. In its second year, it sends up flowering stems that can reach 1-2 feet tall, topped with clusters of small, bright yellow flowers. This member of the mustard family has a peppery, watercress-like flavor and was historically grown as a salad green. The plant has a somewhat sprawling growth habit and can form patches in suitable locations.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green leaves are deeply divided into rounded lobes, with the terminal lobe being the largest. They feel smooth and somewhat thick, and have a sharp, peppery taste when crushed between your teeth - similar to watercress but slightly milder.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers appear in dense, flat-topped clusters. Each flower has four petals arranged in a cross shape, typical of the mustard family. The flowers are quite small, about 1/4 inch across, but very numerous.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading rosettes in the first year, then sends up branching flowering stems in the second year. The plant tends to hug the ground initially, creating dense mats of foliage.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces narrow, upright seed pods (siliques) that are about an inch long. These pods split open when ripe to release small, dark seeds. The pods stand erect on short stalks above the flower clusters.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flowering stems are smooth, somewhat succulent, and branch repeatedly. They feel hollow when squeezed gently and have a crisp texture that snaps cleanly when broken.

habitat: Land cress thrives in moist, rich soils along stream banks, in wet meadows, and at the edges of springs or seeps. It prefers partially shaded areas with consistent moisture but good drainage, often growing alongside watercress in similar habitats. You might find it in disturbed areas like roadside ditches or the edges of cultivated fields where water collects.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early and flower buds begin forming. This is when the leaves are most tender and flavorful for eating, before the plant puts energy into flowering.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom prolifically from late spring through summer. The plant is most conspicuous during this time when the cheerful flower clusters are easily spotted.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and disperse, while new rosettes may form for overwintering. Older flowering stems begin to die back, but basal leaves often remain green.
seasonality.winter: In milder areas, rosettes of leaves may persist through winter, staying green under snow cover. The plant essentially goes dormant but can resume growth during warm spells.

funFact: Land cress was specifically cultivated in England starting in the 1600s as a 'dry weather watercress' - when droughts made it impossible to grow watercress in streams, gardeners could still harvest this peppery green from regular garden beds, earning it the nickname 'upland cress.'
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with bitter wintercress, but land cress has more rounded leaf lobes and a milder, less bitter taste. Memory trick: 'Land cress is less bitter' - if it makes your face pucker when you taste a small piece, it's probably bitter wintercress instead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'American cress' in some regions, land cress is actually native to southern Europe and western Asia, not North America. It was brought here as a cultivated vegetable and has since naturalized in suitable habitats throughout New England.
compareHints: Land cress differs from bitter wintercress by having more rounded, less deeply cut leaf lobes and a milder flavor. Unlike American yellowrocket, land cress tends to stay lower to the ground and has darker green foliage. Small-flowered winter-cress has much smaller, less showy flowers and more finely divided leaves than land cress.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Bitter wintercress has the largest, most rounded terminal leaf lobe compared to its relatives.
Small-flowered winter-cress stands out from other wintercresses primarily by its diminutive flowers - they're about half the size of bitter wintercress blooms.
Among its wintercress relatives in New England, American yellowrocket is distinguished by its more compact growth habit and distinctly oval, less-divided leaves.
